content: The Betel plant, scientifically known as Piper betle, is a spice with leaves that possess medicinal properties. It is an evergreen and perennial plant characterized by glossy, heart-shaped leaves and white catkins, and it typically grows to a height of approximately one meter. The plant is native to Malaysia but is now cultivated in India, Indonesia, and Sri Lanka. Among the various types of Betel leaves, the Magahi variety, grown near Patna in Bihar, India, is considered the finest. The plant is referred to by different names in various regions, such as Vetrilai in Tamil and Vettila in Malayalam. The active components of Betel oil, which is extracted from the leaves, primarily belong to a class of allylbenzene compounds. These include chavibetol (betel-phenol; 3-hydroxy-4-methoxyallylbenzene), chavicol (p-allyl-phenol; 4-allyl-phenol), estragole (p-allyl-anisole; 4-methoxy-allylbenzene), eugenol (allylguaiacol; 4-hydroxy-3-methoxy-allylbenzene), methyl eugenol (eugenol methyl ether; 3,4-dimethoxy-allylbenzene), and hydroxycatechol (2,4-dihydroxy-allylbenzene). Additionally, Betel oil contains several terpenes and terpenoids, including two monoterpenes (p-cymene and terpinene), two monoterpenoids (eucalyptol and carvacrol), and two sesquiterpenes (cadinene and caryophyllene). In India and parts of Southeast Asia, Betel leaves are commonly chewed along with slaked lime (calcium hydroxide) and the areca nut, which is often mistakenly referred to as the Betel nut. The slaked lime helps maintain the active ingredient in its freebase or alkaline form, facilitating its absorption into the bloodstream through sublingual absorption. The areca nut contains the alkaloid arecoline, which stimulates salivation (resulting in red-stained saliva) and acts as a stimulant. This combination, known as a Betel quid, has been used for thousands of years. Tobacco is sometimes added to the mixture. Betel leaves are traditionally used as a stimulant, an antiseptic, and a breath freshener. In Ayurvedic medicine, they are also considered an aphrodisiac. In Malaysia, Betel leaves are used to treat headaches, arthritis, and joint pain. In Thailand, Indonesia, and China, they are employed to alleviate toothaches. In Indonesia, Betel leaves are consumed as an infusion and used as an antibiotic. They are also used in infusions to treat indigestion, as a topical remedy for constipation, as a decongestant, and as an aid to lactation. In India, Betel leaves are used to expel intestinal worms. Betel and areca play a significant role in Indian culture, particularly among Hindus. They are integral to traditional ceremonies, such as offerings to priests, where money is placed in Betel leaves as a form of payment. Similarly, Betel and areca hold cultural importance in Vietnam. A Vietnamese saying, the Betel begins the conversation, highlights the use of Betel chewing in formal occasions or to ease awkward social interactions. Betel leaves and areca nuts are also ceremonially used in traditional Vietnamese weddings, symbolizing love and marriage. According to a folk tale, the groom traditionally offers Betel leaves and areca nuts to the bride's parents as part of the marriage proposal. In Vietnamese culture, the phrase matters of Betel and areca is synonymous with marriage. A related plant, Piper sarmentosum, which is used in cooking, is sometimes referred to as wild Betel leaf. Warning: Chewing Betel has been associated with an increased risk of oral and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
